Events, reducers and analysis outputs

Source: vignettes/v04_extraction.Rmd
v04_extraction.Rmd

These 2.10.4 examples use the integrated recipe-language-2 implementation. They are not evaluated during documentation builds because they need live DataSHIELD connections and study-specific vocabulary inputs. Patient tables are assigned beside the data; use reviewed DataSHIELD methods to analyse them. The previous chapter explains populations and index dates.

Choose rows, then columns

The simple layer is enough for baseline values around an index. Define concept sets for your vocabulary; the following IDs illustrate a diabetes study.

library(dsOMOPClient)
index <- omop_event("condition_occurrence", 201826, descendants = TRUE)
study <- omop_study(
  index = index, require = list(age = c(18, NA)),
  baseline = list(age = omop_age(), sex = omop_sex(),
    hba1c = omop_value_at_index("measurement", 3004410,
                               tolerance = c(-90, 30), unit = 8554),
    visits = omop_count("visit_occurrence", before = 365)),
  outputs = "baseline")
recipe_to_code(study)

before = 365 includes days -365 through 0; after = 30 includes days 1 through 30. Choose only one of before, after and window. Without one, shortcuts use all history through index day. A numeric unit restricts rows to that unit; it does not convert values. omop_unit() supplies explicit affine conversions, applied before predicates and reducers.

Education level and cause of death in one wide table

An education question is the observation’s observation_concept_id; the answer (primary, secondary, and so on) is value_as_concept_id. Choose the question’s concept ID from the site’s vocabulary. education_question below is that study input, not a universal education code.

The familiar table/format spelling remains available:

education <- omop_variable(
  name = "education", table = "observation", concept_id = education_question,
  value_source = "value_as_concept_id", type = "categorical", format = "last_value")
cause <- omop_variable(name = "cause_of_death", table = "death",
  column = "cause_concept_id", type = "categorical", format = "first_value")

The advanced spelling names an event and reducer. This selects the last coded answer through the index day, avoiding post-index education updates:

education_event <- omop_event("observation", concepts = education_question)
education <- omop_variable(name = "education", event = education_event,
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id",
                         window = omop_window(NULL, 0), missing = "skip"))
cause <- omop_variable(name = "cause_of_death", event = omop_event("death"),
  reducer = omop_reduce("first_value", value = "cause_concept_id"))
pop <- omop_population(id = "patients", index = omop_index(index))
recipe <- omop_recipe(
  populations = list(patients = pop),
  variables = list(education = education, cause_of_death = cause),
  outputs = list(profile = omop_output("profile", format = "wide",
    rows = "patients", grain = "episode",
    columns = c("education", "cause_of_death"))),
  options = list(translate_concepts = TRUE))
recipe_explain(recipe, conns = conns)
result <- recipe_execute(recipe, out = c(profile = "D_profile"), conns = conns)

Translation follows the declared concept type, including renamed wide columns; it does not depend on an _concept_id suffix. The assigned columns are unordered factors with shared permitted levels. Joins and computations use internal IDs; the published labels are presentation. To retain numeric concept IDs instead, set options = list(translate_concepts = FALSE) on the recipe. cause_of_death is the coded cause, not proof that everyone has died; missing cause stays NA. It is an outcome description and may use future information, so do not treat it as a pre-index predictor.

For a dataset that stores answers as text, this spelling illustrates the requested alternative, but it is deliberately refused under ordinary policy:

education_text <- omop_variable(name = "education_text", table = "observation",
  concept_id = education_question, value_source = "value_as_string",
  type = "categorical", format = "last_value")
# recipe_to_plan() refuses a recipe that releases this class-1 source.

value_as_string and cause_source_value are free source text (class 1). Selecting a categorical type or renaming the column does not make them safe. Use coded value_as_concept_id and cause_concept_id for the portable recipe. An administrator’s existing sensitive-column override is not permission to use text predicates or to alias protected source columns through mutation.

Declare labels and keep complete categories

Use study-reviewed concept IDs as the names of a public labels map. Variable maps override recipe maps; equal labels deliberately combine categories. This example uses illustrative gender IDs, which must be checked for your CDM:

gender <- omop_variable(name = "gender", table = "person",
  column = "gender_concept_id", type = "categorical", format = "raw",
  labels = c(`8507` = "Male", `8532` = "Female"))

column_names maps stable untranslated generated column keys to complete R names. It renames columns without combining them; duplicate target names are refused. Automatic duplicate concept names are disambiguated by ID. Empty labels are refused, while a literal "NA" is a category distinct from missing. Keep the default factor_concepts = TRUE when translation is enabled.

After publishing the education recipe above, use its committed symbol for a pooled table that retains every permitted category, including unused levels:

ds.omop.table("D_profile", "education", conns = conns)

This helper preserves commas and other literal label text and excludes actual missing values. A failed or suppressed site count causes refusal, never a zero substitution. Direct dsBaseClient::ds.table() can omit globally unused levels. Concept factors keep their shared levels during model-frame subsetting; other packages still need their own reviewed methods and model compatibility checks.

Derived sex uses the public F, M factor domain. Age bands, birth-year bands and calendar categories are ordered factors, including unused declared levels. Ordered factors use ordered contrasts in R models; choose your model coding explicitly. Use as.character() for labels, not integer factor codes as values. CSV and Parquet staging preserve levels and order; read them through the staged descriptor contract rather than treating the CSV file as an ordinary download.

Dates, calendar periods and age at an event

Native date helpers separate the date source from its presentation. A recipe date_spec supplies defaults; each variable overrides the fields it declares. These are variables that can be included in a wide output like education above:

visit_quarter <- omop_date("first_visit",
  omop_date_spec(precision = "quarter",
    level_range = c("2010-01-01", "2030-12-31")))
visit_trend <- omop_date("first_visit",
  omop_date_spec(precision = "month", representation = "number",
    origin = "2010-01-01"))
visit_start <- omop_date("first_visit",
  omop_date_spec(precision = "quarter", representation = "start"))
visit_parts <- omop_date_parts("first_visit",
  c(visit_year = "year", visit_month = "month", weekday = "weekday"))
age_at_death <- omop_age_at("death")
followup_days <- omop_time_between("index", "observation_end", unit = "days")

Calendar periods default to ordered factors. number provides a trend coordinate; start and end provide inclusive Date bounds. level_range declares additional public levels, including unused middle years; it never filters observed dates. Names use fixed English. ISO week labels use %G-W%V, not %Y-W%V; custom patterns use a closed directive set. Fiscal calendars and explicitly profiled epidemiological weeks are available in omop_date_spec().

omop_age_at() counts completed anniversaries at its own reference date; February 29 birthdays use March 1 in non-leap years. Incomplete birth dates return NA unless an explicit imputation is chosen. unit = "annual_years" requests calendar-year age instead. Legacy omop_age() remains annual age, and omitted native specifications preserve legacy first/last-date offsets. An explicit omop_date_spec() on a first/last-date reducer selects native Date presentation. Do not overlap a native specification with legacy date_handling.

For a reproducible future-date policy, use omop_date_spec(future = "na", as_of = "2026-01-01"). The policy applies after row selection: a selected later date becomes NA; it does not substitute an earlier event. Invalid dates remain missing. Exact-date assignment needs no dsomop.allow_absolute_dates opt-in. Date-derived columns retain class-2 provenance, final person support and all downstream aggregate controls.

Understand the reducer

A reducer summarizes an event stream per person or episode. Count and binary return zero for an available empty stream. Value reducers return NA; a sum returns zero. Unavailable sources and undefined required anchors yield NA, including for counts. first_value and last_value select one complete row by date and deterministic source key; missing = "skip" skips missing values before selection, whereas keep retains the selected row’s missing value. Selected value, unit, operator and date must refer to the same row.

rx <- omop_event("drug_exposure", 1503297, descendants = TRUE)
era <- omop_era(rx, gap = 30, persistence = 0)
covered <- omop_variable(event = era,
  reducer = omop_reduce("covered_days", window = omop_window(1, 365),
                         observed_only = TRUE))
observed <- omop_observed_days(omop_window(1, 365))

Course duration includes grace and persistence; covered_days unions recorded coverage and excludes those gaps. With observed_only = TRUE, the numerator and observed_days denominator use the same observed days. Thus PDC can be computed as covered/observed, with a zero denominator becoming NA. MPR uses supply_days, not duration_sum; overlapping supplies have different meanings in those measures. Stockpiling exposes a separate effective_supply relation that must be selected explicitly. Native comorbidity scores use conditions through their reference date (the episode index by default); a consumer with no unique index needs a fixed date.

Choose an output shape

Shape Intended use
wide One row per declared person or episode; selected variables become columns.
long Event rows from sources; a reducer needs broadcast = TRUE to repeat over them.
survival Named TAR components; first event, competing risk, recurrent events, counting process or multi-state as declared.
intervals Recorded or constructed intervals.
person_period Dense or sparse panels with explicit bins and source identities.
temporal_covariates, sparse Covariate rows plus reference companions.
membership, dictionary Patient membership, or plan/vocabulary reference metadata respectively.
joined A declared, validated composition of private inputs.

An indexed population requires episode grain unless a person-grain output explicitly collapses episodes (first_episode, last_episode or any). A dense available-but-event-free source keeps its declared columns and zero/NA rules; an unavailable source is NA. Multi-concept source columns retain concept identity. Carry-forward is per source and concept, evaluated at period start.

Survival windows and censoring are explicit. Native v2 adds no implicit cohort-end cap; request index_end when intended. A named TAR yields its own inventory entry, such as D_tte.itt. Each independently accessible patient component must pass distinct-person support; a passing roster does not permit a small event component to escape. Reference companions are released only with their passing family.

Publish and analyse 

recipe <- recipe_set_publish(recipe, "profile")
result <- recipe_execute(recipe, out = c(profile = "D_profile"),
                         output_mode = "memory", conns = conns)
# Use the symbols in result's committed inventory for downstream analysis.
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_profile", datasources = conns)

# Assigned ordinary analysis columns can be transformed server-side.
ds.omop.mutate("D_profile", has_cause = !is.na(cause_of_death),
                newobj = "D_profile_derived", conns = conns)
ds.omop.filter("D_profile_derived", expr = omop_where(has_cause == TRUE),
                newobj = "D_deaths", conns = conns)

Fresh names may differ when destinations already exist. Verbs publish a new patient object and recheck its own support; mutations cannot read or write person, episode or set keys. They use a closed expression language, not arbitrary R. In-place mutation (newobj = x) keeps a rollback copy until federation commit is verified and invalidates DP provenance.

Staged mode writes private server-local Parquet (CSV fallback) and returns validated descriptors, not download URLs. A server-side consumer resolves a committed component with omopStagedDatasetPath(). Uncommitted or revoked components are unreadable. Keep the returned dynamic inventory rather than predicting component suffixes.

Exact birth components and exact age may be assigned on request. Assigned age bands accept any increasing integer grid starting at zero, including c(0, 18, 19, 65), without per-band suppression. Aggregate endpoints retain their existing admission, banding and suppression rules; a permitted assigned column does not grant an unrestricted aggregate release.
